A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VAREdit/SAR research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original VAREdit evaluations on EMU-Edit and PIE-Bench, conditioning ablations and attention analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional benchmark evaluations, diagnostic analyses, qualitative experiments and a human preference study.

M1.justification: Both versions use Infinity-based next-scale prediction, finest-scale source conditioning and downsampled SAR references in the first self-attention layer. v2 elaborates the existing quantizer and bitwise loss; model renaming and longer training do not establish an algorithm or architecture change.

E1.justification: Beyond EMU-Edit and PIE-Bench, v2 evaluates ImgEdit-Bench's basic and understanding-grounding-editing suites and GEdit-Bench's English subset. Appendix A.5 adds imaginative, implicit-reasoning, sequential multi-turn and ambiguous/conflicting-instruction scenarios. Appendix A.1 also reports proprietary editing samples for large-model training, although their composition is unspecified.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains all seven original comparators and adds Step1X-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext (dev), Qwen-Image-Edit and GPT-4o-Image on the existing EMU-Edit and PIE-Bench comparisons. This substantially strengthens the comparison set.

E3.justification: The large model's stated training budget changes from 26k to 60k iterations. v2 introduces benchmark-specific GPT rating protocols, preservation analysis restricted to GPT-Success scores of at least 9, attention averaging across PIE-Bench samples and heads, and a randomized three-way preference study with five participants. The original small-model training settings remain.

E4.justification: The original Full/Finest/SAR ablation is retained. v2 substantially expands mechanism evidence with benchmark-averaged, full-layer and SAR-specific attention maps, tests preservation conditional on successful editing, adds human preference validation, and examines ambiguous instructions, multi-turn behavior and concrete failure cases.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for model comparisons. The new human study reports average wins and preference rates without uncertainty estimates; its participant count and randomization are evaluation-design additions.

E6.justification: Under revised training and data, the large model's GPT-Balance entries change from 6.773 to 7.892 on EMU-Edit and from 7.298 to 8.105 on PIE-Bench. New comparisons place GPT-4o-Image and Qwen-Image-Edit above VAREdit on this metric. Additional benchmark and human-preference results appear, and OmniGen scores change slightly. Small-model and original conditioning-ablation scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit componentwise BSQ quantizer definition in Appendix A.4, Equation 8, and revises query/key transpose placement in Equation 7. The core factorization, SAR reference construction and positional-coordinate formulas remain, without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain next-scale image editing, SAR conditioning and editing-quality/efficiency advantages. The introduction narrows the priority claim from 'the first' to 'among the first.' The abstract replaces the quantified GPT-Balance advantage with a broader claim covering both CLIP and GPT scores on the named benchmarks.

C2.justification: v1 mainly discusses small-model weaknesses and benefits of scaling. v2 adds interpretations of generalization, ambiguous-instruction behavior and human preferences, discusses quality versus latency against frontier models, and identifies persistent compositional/anatomical failures. Appendix A.5 also hypothesizes processing-scale density and data coverage as explanations for these limitations.

D1.justification: v2 makes the existing bitwise training objective, quantizer formula and placement of RoPE explicit. It also discloses proprietary large-model training data without specifying its size, composition or access. Existing tokenizer dimensions, scale grids, positional offsets, guidance settings and filtering/evaluation prompts are largely retained.

R1.justification: Related work expands beyond the earlier EditAR-focused discussion to MLLM-assisted editing, NEP, in-context autoregressive editing, and reasoning and efficiency research. Frontier editing approaches receive substantive treatment, and the novelty positioning is qualified from first-of-its-kind to among the first.

P1.justification: Most of the existing narrative and section order remain recognizable. v2 polishes prose, expands methodological explanations, introduces numbered subsection and appendix hierarchies, shortens model names to 2B/8B, and adds conference, correspondence and acknowledgement text. Much of the expansion is new scientific content rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, redraws the architecture diagram and attention displays, and adds successful-edit scatter plots, extensive qualitative panels and benchmark/user-study tables. Existing categorical tables and qualitative comparisons are retained and renumbered; the ablation table gains input-length and timing columns.

improvement.justification: Benchmark-wide attention maps and success-conditioned preservation analysis strengthen evidence that was narrower in v1; stronger comparators and explicit failure cases also improve practical assessment. However, unspecified proprietary training data for the large model weakens reproducibility and attribution of its updated scores. The five-participant study also interprets a 36.0% versus 33.9% preference lead strongly without uncertainty analysis, tempering the overall benefit.
